title: Did a Dead Jockey Really Win This Horse Race?
description:
On June 4, 1923, a stable hand named Frank Hayes got his first ride in a real race: a steeplechase at Belmont Park, New York, on his boss's mare, Sweet Kiss. He starved himself to make the weight. The long shot won. And Frank never got off her alive.

For a hundred years the story has been told one way: a dead man rode a horse across the finish line. This is what the newspapers from that week actually said, and why nobody can say exactly when his heart stopped.

Chapters
0:00 Cold open
0:28 The stable hand
0:57 What a steeplechase is
1:34 Making the weight
2:15 The race
2:50 Past the post
3:15 The legend
4:08 The win counted

Facts used: Frank Hayes worked with horses as a stable hand and trainer for the Frayling family; his mother told a newspaper he had loved horses since childhood. On June 4, 1923, he rode the mare Sweet Kiss, entered in the name of Miss A. M. Frayling, in a steeplechase of about two miles at Belmont Park, just outside New York City. The favorite was Gimme; accounts since give Sweet Kiss's odds anywhere from 5-1 to 20-1. Sweet Kiss was set to carry 130 pounds and Frank was more than ten pounds over, so he stopped eating, jogged for hours and, a Buffalo paper reported, went without water; he lost more than ten pounds in about a day. The Buffalo Courier (June 5, 1923) reported that after the last fence he was seen swaying in the saddle, dipped to one side and recovered; Sweet Kiss won easily; he rode on toward the judges' stand and fell from the saddle before attendants reached him. The track's doctor found him dead; the papers blamed heart failure brought on by the weight loss. The New York Times headline: "Jockey Dies as He Wins His First Race." His age is given as 22 in most accounts today and 35 in a paper at the time. The widely shared photo of a slumped jockey is not him: it shows a 1933 race in Sydney, Australia, and no photo of Frank riding Sweet Kiss is known. We found no proof that Sweet Kiss never raced again or was called "the Sweet Kiss of Death." The win stood. He was buried three days later at Holy Cross Cemetery in Brooklyn, in his racing silks.

The scenes are an animated dramatization.

comment: Did Frank Hayes win that race alive... or did a dead man cross the line?
